subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage: Okay, so in Class Ten I was sure everyone hated me. It started in the canteen queue: three girls from my section looked at me, looked at each other, then looked away. I went home certain they were laughing at my haircut. For two days I sat at the back and wouldn't lift my eyes. Then you, Wasim, cornered me at the water cooler and said, "Suraj, why are you avoiding everybody?" I told you. You said, "Just ask them, yaar." So I did, red in the face. One of them said, "We wanted you on our quiz team but we were too shy to ask." 😅 I've never felt so silly. Now I check before I decide.

qa.q: Where did the three girls look at Suraj and then away?
qa.a: They looked at him in the canteen queue.

qa.q: Why did Suraj sit at the back and not lift his eyes for two days?
qa.a: He was certain the girls were laughing at his haircut, so he felt embarrassed and wanted to avoid being looked at. The glances could have meant many things, but he only imagined the worst.

qa.q: What could Suraj do the next time someone glances at him and looks away?
qa.a: He could check the facts first, by asking a friend or the person kindly, before deciding it means gossip. Asking took him two days to try but cleared it up in a minute.

qa.q: How might the girls have felt while they were looking and looking away?
qa.a: They were shy about inviting him to the quiz team, so looking away was nervousness, not judgement. They may not have known he was watching them.

grounding: A teenager reads sideways glances as gossip, then checks the facts and finds shyness.

subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage: I sit behind Abhinav in maths, so I saw the whole thing. Some girls by the window kept glancing over during the test review, and he noticed. His shoulders went up and his pen stopped moving. At lunch he muttered, "They're talking about my marks." I said, "Or your shirt, or nothing." He nearly walked off. Then he went straight over and asked, "Were you looking at me?" One girl said, "Your pencil box has the same sticker as mine, I wanted to ask where you got it." He laughed and his shoulders dropped. I'm Yusuf, and I can't say what was going on inside him, but I think he'd been scared for two periods.

qa.q: Where do Yusuf and Abhinav sit in relation to each other in maths?
qa.a: Yusuf sits behind Abhinav in maths.

qa.q: What was Abhinav probably worried about when he saw the glances?
qa.a: He probably worried the girls were talking about his marks. His raised shoulders and stopped pen fit that, though Yusuf admits he cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What could Abhinav try if he notices glances again?
qa.a: He can do what he did at lunch: ask calmly whether they were looking at him, and hear the reason before assuming. A friend nearby can also offer other possible reasons.

qa.q: How does the girl by the window see the situation?
qa.a: She was only curious about the sticker and wanted to ask about it. She may have been surprised that a glance caused worry.

grounding: A teenager reads sideways glances as gossip, and asking directly shows a harmless reason, as seen by an observer.

subtype: Blushing cheeks and raised cheeks [Mismatch]
passage: Karthik, come and sit. I'm Asif, and when I was fifteen, I won the school elocution prize, and the headmaster announced my name in the assembly with two hundred children watching. My cheeks went hot. Rafiq, who sat next to me, whispered, "Look at you beaming!" I was smiling, yes, but I also wanted the floor to open up. The cheeks give you away, and you can't argue with them. Then our English teacher came over and said quietly, "Come, drink some water, the clapping will be over soon," and didn't say anything about my face. I've never forgotten that. Later Rafiq told me he'd thought I was purely thrilled. I told him it was both.

qa.q: How many children were watching Asif when his name was announced?
qa.a: Two hundred children were watching in the assembly.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when his cheeks went hot?
qa.a: He was happy and embarrassed at once. He smiled, yet also wanted the floor to open up, so Rafiq's reading of pure joy was only half right.

qa.q: How can a teacher or friend help someone whose cheeks redden in public?
qa.a: They can offer a small kind action, like water and a quiet word, and avoid remarks about the face. That gives the person room to settle.

qa.q: How did Rafiq read Asif's face, and why might he have been wrong?
qa.a: Rafiq saw beaming and assumed Asif was thrilled. Red cheeks and a smile can come from joy or embarrassment, so Rafiq needed context or a question to know.

grounding: A teenager's red cheeks mix joy and embarrassment, others read it from context, and kindness spares him.

subtype: Blushing cheeks and raised cheeks [Mismatch]
passage: The bus to school was packed and the rain had steamed every window, so Anjali had nowhere to turn her face. Behind her, two classmates were reading out a compliment someone had written about her drawing. "Whoever wrote it clearly likes you!" Her cheeks burned, and she couldn't stop the corners of her mouth lifting either. She hoped nobody could tell if she was pleased or mortified. Joseph, holding the same rail, saw her face and said loudly, "Did anyone finish the chemistry sheet? I'm stuck on question four." The classmates groaned and started arguing about it. Anjali let out a breath. She caught his eye and mouthed a quick thank you 🙂

qa.q: What had the rain done to the windows of the bus?
qa.a: The rain had steamed every window.

qa.q: What might Anjali have been feeling with burning cheeks and lifting mouth corners?
qa.a: She was likely pleased and embarrassed together. Her lifted mouth suggests pleasure, and the burning cheeks with hiding her face suggest embarrassment.

qa.q: What small step helped Anjali in the crowded bus?
qa.a: Joseph changed the subject by asking about the chemistry sheet. That took attention off her face without making a fuss.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have spoken loudly rather than privately to Anjali?
qa.a: In a packed bus a whisper could not stop the classmates, and a loud question moved everyone's attention away. He may also have wanted to avoid pointing at her blush.

grounding: A teenager's cheeks redden and lift at once in a crowded bus, and a friend's kindness spares her.

subtype: Disgust nose wrinkle at peers [Regulating]
passage: At lunch under the neem tree in Maria's village school, Simran opened her tiffin and unwrapped a jar of her grandmother's sour mango pickle. The smell was strong. Maria's nose wrinkled before she could stop it. She saw Simran's smile slip. Maria breathed in, then said, "The smell is a bit much for me, I'm not used to it. But the colour is beautiful. Can I try just a little?" Simran laughed with relief and gave her a tiny piece on a leaf. Maria tasted it, coughed, and said, "Too sour for me, honestly, but thank you for sharing." Simran said, "Nani says that too." They shared the rotis instead.

qa.q: What did Simran unwrap from her tiffin?
qa.a: She unwrapped a jar of her grandmother's sour mango pickle.

qa.q: Why did Maria's face change and then she spoke up?
qa.a: Maria's nose wrinkled from the strong smell, then she noticed Simran's smile slip and did not want to hurt her friend. She chose kind, honest words instead of a silent sneer.

qa.q: What could Maria do if she didn't want to try the pickle at all?
qa.a: She could say kindly that it isn't for her and thank Simran for offering. Honest words, said warmly, respect both of them.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt if Maria had only kept the wrinkled nose?
qa.a: Simran might have felt judged and hurt about something her grandmother made. A spoken reason left her laughing with relief.

grounding: A teenager wrinkles her nose at a smell, then softens it with kind honest words.

subtype: Disgust nose wrinkle at peers [Regulating]
passage: After PE in a Toronto school locker room, Olga sprayed a cloud of new perfume and grinned. "Smell it! My aunt gave it to me." Yuki's nose wrinkled hard, the smell was stinging her throat. She saw Olga watching her face. "Do you hate it?" Olga asked, smile fading. Yuki thought for a second. "It's really strong for me in a small room, that's all. I like that it's from your aunt. Maybe one spray, not five?" Olga glanced at the bottle. "Oh. I did overdo it." She opened the window and laughed. "One spray, then. Deal." 😊

qa.q: Where did Olga spray the new perfume?
qa.a: She sprayed it in the school locker room after PE.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when her nose wrinkled, and why did she add a kind comment?
qa.a: She felt disgust at the stinging smell but also cared about Olga's feelings. That is why she mentioned the aunt and suggested fewer sprays.

qa.q: What would you advise Yuki if the smell bothered her again?
qa.a: She could say it kindly and early, like she did, and offer a small fix. Being honest in words works better than pulling a face.

qa.q: What is it like for Olga when Yuki's face changes?
qa.a: Olga sees the nose wrinkle and feels her happiness drop, so she asks directly. When Yuki explains, she can laugh and fix it.

grounding: A teenager wrinkles her nose at a smell but softens it with kind honest words to spare her friend.

subtype: Lip biting when unsure or anxious [Regulating]
passage: In the changing room after training, Mateo kept biting his lower lip. The coach had put him in defence for the semi-final, and he badly wanted the striker spot back, but he didn't want to sound like he was complaining. Fatima, tying her boots, noticed the lip. "You've got that lip thing again. Something you want to say?" Mateo let go and rubbed his mouth. "I don't know. Maybe. I want to ask the coach, but I'm afraid of sounding selfish." Fatima shrugged gently. "Asking isn't selfish. I can come with you if you like." He nodded slowly, a tiny weight coming off his chest.

qa.q: Which position had the coach given Mateo for the semi-final?
qa.a: The coach had put him in defence.

qa.q: What might Mateo be afraid of as he bites his lip?
qa.a: He wanted to ask for the striker spot back but was afraid of sounding selfish. Biting his lip held the words in while he felt nervous.

qa.q: What could Mateo try before speaking to the coach?
qa.a: He could plan a few calm words about what he'd like and why, and take Fatima up on coming along. A short, honest request is easier than swallowing it.

qa.q: How does Fatima see his lip biting?
qa.a: She sees it as a sign there's something he wants to say, so she asks gently. Noticing without pushing let him decide to talk.

grounding: A teenager bites his lip to hold back words while nervous, and a friend's gentle question opens it up.

subtype: Lip biting when unsure or anxious [Regulating]
passage: Zainab sat on the bench outside the principal's office, waiting for her scholarship interview. Her lower lip was caught between her teeth. She'd rehearsed her answers on the bus, but now every sentence had gone blank. Aditi, who had come to wait with her, glanced over. "You're biting your lip so hard it's going white." Zainab let go. "I'm scared I'll say something silly." "Do you want to go through the first question again?" Aditi asked. They ran it twice, whispering. When the door opened, Zainab stood, took a slow breath, and pressed her lips together into a small, steady smile.

qa.q: Where was Zainab waiting for her interview?
qa.a: She sat on the bench outside the principal's office.

qa.q: What was Zainab worried about while she bit her lip?
qa.a: She was scared she would say something silly, and her mind had gone blank. Her lip biting shows she was holding herself in and calming her nerves.

qa.q: What small step helped Zainab before the door opened?
qa.a: Aditi offered to go through the first question again, and they practised it twice in whispers. Practice and a slow breath eased her nerves.

qa.q: What is it like for Aditi noticing her friend's lip?
qa.a: Aditi could see the tension and asked gently instead of pretending not to notice. She may worry a little herself but chooses to help.

grounding: A teenager bites her lip to calm nerves, and a friend notices and offers gentle support.

subtype: Pouting and pursing for cameras and moods [Mismatch]
passage: At the mela, Hrithik took selfies by the tea stall with his lips pushed out in a big pout. "Model!" his friends teased, and he posed again, grinning. Pankaj stood a little apart with his lips pressed together, looking at the ground. Hrithik snapped a photo. "Ha, duck face! Now you're copying me." Pankaj didn't laugh. "I'm not posing," he said. "Coach dropped me from the team list today." Hrithik's grin fell. He put the phone in his pocket. "Sorry. I thought that was for the camera. Want to sit?" Pankaj nodded, and Hrithik bought two teas.

qa.q: Where did Hrithik take selfies?
qa.a: He took selfies by the tea stall at the mela.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when his lips pressed together?
qa.a: He was hurt about being dropped from the team list. His downcast eyes and quiet tone show sadness, not a pose.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Hrithik took Pankaj's sulk for posing and joked. Asking first, or stopping when Pankaj stayed silent, would have avoided the sting.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik react differently once he hears the news?
qa.a: He first read the pursed lips as style because that was his own mood. After hearing Pankaj, he sees the context and shifts to kindness.

grounding: A teenager pouts for a camera while a friend's pursed lips are real hurt, and mocking it deepens the hurt.

subtype: Pouting and pursing for cameras and moods [Mismatch]
passage: Beatriz held her phone at arm's length, chin tilted, lips pushed into a pout. The photo was for the group chat. Across the terrace, Ivan saw her pouting and assumed she was upset about something. "Hey, what happened?" he asked, coming over. She burst out laughing. "Nothing! It's my photo face." "Oh. I thought you were sulking about the football." "I'm sulking about your terrible taste in shirts 😄" she said. Ivan grinned and held out his hand for the phone. "Let me see it." She showed him, and he said it looked good, but he preferred her real laugh.

qa.q: What did Beatriz say her pout was for?
qa.a: She said it was her photo face, for the group chat.

qa.q: What did Ivan think Beatriz was feeling when he saw her pout, and what does his question suggest?
qa.a: Ivan thought she was upset or sulking. He asked instead of joking, which shows he was unsure and cared.

qa.q: What did Ivan choose to do that worked well?
qa.a: He asked what was wrong instead of teasing her. Asking cleared it up without hurting anyone.

qa.q: How might Beatriz feel about Ivan's question?
qa.a: She may feel cared for that he checked. It could also feel funny that a style was read as a mood.

grounding: A teenager's pout is a style for a selfie, not a sulk, and a friend checks by asking.

subtype: Clenched jaw under pressure [Regulating]
passage: Ten minutes left, the ceiling fan had stopped, and Sarika was stuck on the last long question. Her jaw was clenched so hard her teeth ached. She wanted to shout that the paper was unfair, but she pressed her lips together. She put the pen down, opened her jaw slowly, moved it side to side, and took a long breath in and out. Irawati, beside her, glanced over and gave a small nod. Sarika picked the pen up and wrote the first step she was sure of. When the bell rang, the teacher said quietly, "If you'd like to talk about how it went, I'm around."

qa.q: How many minutes were left when Sarika was stuck on the last question?
qa.a: Ten minutes were left.

qa.q: What is Sarika feeling and wanting as she clenches her jaw?
qa.a: She wanted to shout that the paper was unfair but held it in under pressure. The clenched jaw and pressed lips show tension, though she may also have been frightened of failing.

qa.q: What could Sarika try again when the pressure rises?
qa.a: She can open her jaw slowly, stretch it side to side and breathe out long, as she did. Then she can write the step she is sure of.

qa.q: How might the teacher's offer feel to Sarika?
qa.a: It gives her a choice to talk without pressure. She may feel relieved that no one demanded an answer right away.

grounding: A teenager clenches her jaw in an exam to hold back words, and slow breathing and an adult's low-pressure offer help.

subtype: Clenched jaw under pressure [Regulating]
passage: "You're not getting a phone until your marks come up," Dilnaz said from the kitchen. Zeenat's jaw locked. She had a dozen replies ready, each sharper than the last. She walked to the bathroom, shut the door and ran the tap. In the mirror she saw her clenched jaw. She unclenched it, stretched it wide like a yawn, and breathed out slowly, three times. When she came out, Dilnaz was standing by the door with two cups of tea. "I shouldn't have said it like that. Sit with me?" Zeenat took one. "Can I tell you why I want it?" "Yes," said Dilnaz. "I'm listening."

qa.q: What did Zeenat do after her jaw locked?
qa.a: She walked to the bathroom, shut the door and ran the tap.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as she held back her sharp replies?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated but chose not to say hurtful things. Her locked jaw shows the effort of holding back.

qa.q: What would you advise if a talk gets heated like this?
qa.a: Step away for a moment, stretch the jaw and breathe slowly, then return to talk. Adults can also offer tea and a chance to talk without pressure.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz be feeling when she waits by the door with two cups of tea?
qa.a: She may regret how she said it and want to reconnect. Her apology and question suggest she is ready to listen.

grounding: A teenager clenches her jaw in an argument, uses slow breathing and jaw stretching, and a parent offers to talk.

subtype: Moving the jaw sideways and tongue clicks [Mismatch]
passage: Sunaina, you told me once that when I click my tongue and shift my jaw sideways, I look like I'm judging everyone. I laughed, but it stung. I do it when I'm working out a sum. Nandini clicking equals Nandini thinking, that's all. Then last week the new girl was presenting and I clicked while she talked, and afterwards she asked, "Did I say something wrong?" I felt terrible. I explained, "It's a thinking habit, not a comment on you." She said, "Oh, okay 🙂" Now I try to stay still when someone's speaking, or I say, "I was thinking."

qa.q: When does Nandini click her tongue and shift her jaw?
qa.a: She does it when she's working out a sum.

qa.q: What was the new girl feeling when she asked, "Did I say something wrong?"
qa.a: She was worried that Nandini's click meant disapproval. Her question shows that she read the gesture as dismissive.

qa.q: What could Nandini try to prevent this misunderstanding?
qa.a: She could stay still while someone speaks or say out loud, "I was thinking." A few words make the meaning clear.

qa.q: How does Sunaina see Nandini's habit?
qa.a: Sunaina saw a judging look and said so. The click and jaw shift can look like attitude to someone who does not know the habit.

grounding: A teenager's jaw shift and tongue click mean thinking to her but look dismissive to others.

subtype: Moving the jaw sideways and tongue clicks [Mismatch]
passage: When Mr. Gupta asked the class a question, Saurabh shifted his jaw sideways and clicked his tongue, staring at the ceiling. Two boys behind me muttered, "So rude." I wasn't sure. He doesn't seem like someone who acts like that. After a few seconds he gave a careful answer, and it was right. Later at lunch I saw him do the same jaw shift and click with his best friend, who just grinned and said, "There he goes, solving the universe." I don't know what Saurabh was feeling in class, but I think it might have been thinking. I'm Sonali, and I'm still unsure.

qa.q: Where was Saurabh looking when he clicked his tongue?
qa.a: He was staring at the ceiling.

qa.q: What might Saurabh have been thinking or feeling when he clicked and shifted his jaw?
qa.a: He was most likely thinking about the answer, since he gave a careful and right one afterwards. The click could still have been a dismissive attitude, and Sonali admits she is unsure.

qa.q: What could the two boys do before deciding it was rude?
qa.a: They could wait to see what Saurabh says next or ask him. Judging from a click alone can be unfair.

qa.q: How does Saurabh's best friend see the same gesture?
qa.a: The friend knows him and reads it as thinking, teasing him kindly. Meaning depends on tone and relationship.

grounding: A teenager's jaw shift and tongue click may be thinking or attitude, depending on tone and relationship.

subtype: Poker face and resting face [Regulating]
passage: "Why aren't you smiling? Are you angry at me?" Vidya asked. Raghav blinked. "No! This is just my face. My nani says I look like I'm chewing a lemon." Vidya laughed. "Sorry. I'm keeping mine blank because I'm nervous about the audition." "Really? You look calm." "That's the idea." "Should I stop looking so grumpy?" "No, but I'm glad I asked. I was already planning to avoid you." Raghav grinned. "Then let's both say it out loud next time. Deal?" "Deal." The bell rang. "Break a leg, then," said Raghav, still looking like he was chewing a lemon, and this time Vidya knew it was a kind thing to say. 🙂

qa.q: What does Raghav's nani say he looks like?
qa.a: She says he looks like he's chewing a lemon.

qa.q: What is Vidya feeling behind her blank face?
qa.a: She is nervous about the audition. She holds her face still so nobody can see the nerves, which fits her saying, "That's the idea."

qa.q: What worked in this conversation, and why?
qa.a: Vidya asked instead of guessing, and both then said aloud how they feel. Asking cleared up two misreadings at once.

qa.q: How does Raghav see Vidya's blank face?
qa.a: He thinks she looks calm, so her poker face works. He didn't guess the nerves until she told him.

grounding: A teenager holds a still face to hide nerves while a friend's resting face looks unfriendly, and asking clears both.

subtype: Poker face and resting face [Regulating]
passage: I'm Farhan, and in Class Eleven I decided to keep my face completely blank during the debate, so nobody could see I was nervous. Naveen, sitting next to me, whispered, "You look like you hate this." I said, "I'm fine." "You look like you're about to fight someone." That made me smile a bit, and the tightness eased. After the round, I told him the truth: I was scared and the blank face was armour. He said, "It works, but I couldn't tell if you needed help." Now, when I'm nervous, I tell one friend and keep my face natural.

qa.q: Which class was Farhan in when he decided to keep his face blank?
qa.a: He was in Class Eleven.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling behind his blank face in the debate?
qa.a: He was scared and the blank face was armour to hide it. His smile when Naveen joked shows the tension eased once someone noticed.

qa.q: What could Farhan try in future debates?
qa.a: He can tell one friend he's nervous and let his face stay natural. Telling someone gives them a chance to help.

qa.q: How does Naveen see Farhan's blank face?
qa.a: Naveen sees someone who looks like he hates it or wants to fight, and can't tell if Farhan needs help. The poker face hid both nerves and need.

grounding: A teenager holds a still face to hide nerves, which others misread, and telling a friend helps.

subtype: Tense or rigid face under threat [Interpreting]
passage: The class teacher had just called Sudha out to the corridor, and when she came back her face was completely still. She sat down, stared at the desk and didn't answer when the girl next to her whispered. Mohit watched from two rows behind. Some of the others muttered that she didn't seem to care. But Mohit had heard her mother's name in the teacher's voice, and Sudha's hands were flat and rigid on the desk. He didn't ask questions. At the break he put a bottle of water beside her and said only, "I'm here if you want anyone." She nodded once, without looking up.

qa.q: Where did the class teacher call Sudha before she came back with a still face?
qa.a: The teacher called her out to the corridor.

qa.q: What might Sudha be feeling with her rigid, frozen face?
qa.a: She may be in shock or afraid after upsetting news, since her hands were flat and rigid on the desk. It may look like not caring, but that is only one reading.

qa.q: How could a friend support Sudha without demanding a reaction?
qa.a: Stay nearby, offer something small like water, and say they're there. Give her time to speak when she is ready.

qa.q: How do the other students see Sudha, and how is Mohit different?
qa.a: The others think she doesn't care because her face is still. Mohit notices the rigid hands and reads it as shock, so he waits quietly.

grounding: A teenager reads a friend's frozen face after upsetting news as shock or fear, and offers quiet support.

subtype: Tense or rigid face under threat [Interpreting]
passage: "Yogesh, say something," Swati said gently. He sat on the school steps, face rigid, eyes fixed on the road. A moment earlier his father had called to say the family was moving to another city next month. "You don't even look bothered," said a boy passing by. Swati glared at him. Then she said, "You don't have to say anything. I'll sit here." Yogesh's jaw moved a little. "I can't think," he said at last. "That's okay," said Swati. "We can be quiet." They stayed like that until the bell, and when he stood he whispered, "Thanks for not asking me to feel something." 🤍

qa.q: What news had Yogesh's father just given him?
qa.a: His father said the family was moving to another city next month.

qa.q: What is Yogesh likely feeling behind his rigid face?
qa.a: He is likely in shock or upset, because he says he can't think. His stillness could look like indifference, but his words show it isn't.

qa.q: What would you advise Swati if he stays silent for longer?
qa.a: She can keep offering quiet company without demanding a reaction, and let him speak when he is ready. If it keeps going or worries her, a trusted adult can help.

qa.q: How does the passing boy see Yogesh, and why might he be wrong?
qa.a: He thinks Yogesh isn't bothered because his face shows nothing. A frozen face can mean shock or fear, not indifference.

grounding: A teenager reads a friend's rigid face after upsetting news as shock, and quiet time is better than demanding a reaction.

subtype: Indian head wobble [Mismatch]
passage: Vidya, let me tell you about Elena. Years ago I hosted her, a fifteen-year-old exchange student from Spain, and on day two she asked the auto driver, "Is the fort open today?" He wobbled his head from side to side. She turned to me, worried. "Pranav-ji, is that a no?" I laughed. "Could be yes, could be okay, could be I heard you. Ask again with a word." She tried, "So we can go?" and he said, "Haan, haan, get in." After that she learned to watch the tilt and the smile, and to check when unsure. The wobble was never a no.

qa.q: Where was Elena from?
qa.a: She was a fifteen-year-old exchange student from Spain.

qa.q: What was Elena feeling when the driver wobbled his head?
qa.a: She was worried and unsure, and thought it might be a no. Her question to Pranav shows she couldn't read it.

qa.q: What could a visitor do when unsure about a head wobble?
qa.a: Ask again in words, like "So we can go?", and watch tilt and smile. Checking is better than guessing.

qa.q: How might the auto driver have seen Elena's worry?
qa.a: He probably meant yes or okay and didn't know she took it as a no. He answered happily once she asked with words.

grounding: A teenager in India learns the head wobble can mean yes, okay or I'm listening, and checks in words.

subtype: Indian head wobble [Mismatch]
passage: The railway station was loud and packed, and Imran's train to Pune was due in five minutes. He'd flown in from London two days ago and couldn't find the platform. He asked a porter, "Platform four for Pune?" The porter wobbled his head from side to side and walked off. Imran froze. Was that a no? Parveen, his cousin, caught up. "Head wobble. Could be yes, I heard you, or okay. Ask him with a word." Imran ran after the porter. "So it's platform four, yes?" "Haan, four, four," said the porter, pointing. They made it on with a minute to spare.

qa.q: Where was Imran's train going?
qa.a: His train was going to Pune.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when the porter wobbled his head and walked away?
qa.a: He was confused and anxious because time was short and he couldn't tell yes from no. He froze, which shows how unsure he was.

qa.q: What worked when the gesture was unclear?
qa.a: Imran asked the porter again with clear words, so the meaning was confirmed. Parveen's explanation helped him see the wobble wasn't a clear no.

qa.q: How does Parveen see the head wobble differently from Imran?
qa.a: Parveen grew up with it and knows it can mean yes, I heard you or okay. Imran, new to India, first thought it might be no.

grounding: A teenager in India sees a head wobble that isn't a clear no, and asks in words when unsure.
